help.title: Help
help.intro: How PriceLens works and what the metrics mean.
help.howItWorksBody: Marketplace sellers usually see only basic stats-views, orders. This isn't enough to understand if a specific product makes real money after all expenses: marketplace fees, logistics, ads, returns. PriceLens calculates this for you. You enter product data-price, cost of goods sold (COGS), buyer acquisition costs-and the system shows if the product is profitable at the single unit level. This is unit economics: if one unit generates a profit, your entire business is likely profitable. If it's unprofitable, it's a signal to review your price, costs, or marketing strategy before the issue hits your overall revenue.

metrics.conversion: The percentage of product listing visitors who completed a target action (click, add to cart, or order). A low value is a sign to check listing design, pricing relevance, and ad spend.
metrics.cac: The average cost to acquire one paying customer. High CAC means you should review your marketing strategy; low CAC means you can scale up advertising without risking your economics.
metrics.requiredCpa: The cost per target action-not necessarily a purchase, but the initial interest from a potential customer. High CPA with low CAC usually means ads are targeting the wrong audience.
metrics.ltc: Total variable costs to sell one product: cost of goods sold (COGS), marketplace fees, payment processing, taxes, logistics, expected losses from returns/defects, storage, and packaging.
metrics.cm: The profit from one unit sold after deducting all direct variable costs (excluding advertising). High sales volume won't save you if CM is negative-this metric shows real product profitability, not just turnover.
metrics.ltv: The average lifetime profit generated by a single customer at current sales volumes. Compare this to CAC: if LTV is significantly lower than CAC, customer acquisition is not paying off.
metrics.productRoi: Return on investment for product expenses-how much profit each unit of invested money generates. Helps decide which product is more profitable to promote, even if multiple items yield the same dollar CM.

cm_below.title: CM is below normal
cm_below.subtitle: The item is selling at a loss on a per-unit level
cm_below.whatItMeans: Contribution Margin (CM) is negative-the item's price does not cover even the direct variable costs of selling it: cost of goods sold (COGS), marketplace commission, logistics, and expected losses from returns or defects. Every unit sold reduces business profit, even before accounting for advertising expenses.
cm_below.whyItHappens: Typically, this is due to one or more factors: the price is set below the actual unit economic cost, marketplace commissions or logistics rates increased without a price recalculation, or the return/defect rate turned out higher than initially estimated.
cm_below.whatToDo: Recalculate your COGS including all shipping and storage costs. Raise the price to a level where CM becomes positive, or lower your cost structure-for example, negotiate better logistics terms or reduce the defect rate by improving packaging.

ltv_below.title: LTV is below normal
ltv_below.subtitle: LTV to CAC ratio is less than 1-customer acquisition is not profitable
ltv_below.whatItMeans: The lifetime value of a customer (LTV) is lower than their customer acquisition cost (CAC). Every new customer costs more to acquire than they bring in revenue-this directly leads to a cash flow gap, even if total revenue is growing.
ltv_below.whyItHappens: Most often, this happens due to excessive advertising spend relative to the product's profit margin, low conversion rates from ads to actual purchases, or because the product margin itself is too narrow to sustain active customer acquisition.
ltv_below.whatToDo: Reduce acquisition costs by reviewing your ad channels and targeting settings. Increase the product margin (see CM recommendations), or temporarily limit your advertising budget until the unit economics improve.

ltv_above.title: LTV is above normal
ltv_above.subtitle: LTV to CAC ratio is greater than 5
ltv_above.whatItMeans: The lifetime value of a customer significantly exceeds their acquisition cost. Formally this is a great result, but such a wide gap usually indicates missed growth opportunities rather than just perfect economics.
ltv_above.whyItHappens: Generally, this means you are investing less in advertising than the product's economics allow-either due to low competition in your niche, conservative budgeting, or because the ads are failing to scale for other reasons.
ltv_above.whatToDo: Consider increasing your advertising budget, as the product can justify significantly higher investment than it currently receives. Check if you are hitting ad campaign caps or audience reach limits, and gradually scale up promotion while monitoring changes in the LTV:CAC ratio.
